storyText: On March 22, 2014, a hillside above the North Fork Stillaguamish River near Oso, Washington, collapsed and swept across the valley, burying a neighborhood and State Route 530. It killed 43 people. Could radar from space have shown the hill was moving? And could it watch similar slopes today?
credits: Imagery © Esri · Terrain: AWS Terrain Tiles · Layout preview with placeholder data

why.title: What happened at Oso?
why.body: A steep hillside of glacial sediment on the south side of the North Fork Stillaguamish River failed on March 22, 2014, after a very wet period. The debris crossed the valley, buried a neighborhood and blocked the river and State Route 530. It was the deadliest single landslide in US history.

why.title: Had it moved before?
why.body: Yes. The same hillside had slid in earlier decades. That is why scientists ask whether slow movement before a failure can be seen from space, so that warning signs can be spotted.

why.title: How can radar help?
why.body: Radar measures tiny changes in distance to the ground. A slope that creeps a few centimeters shows up as a smooth pattern in the Fringes view. Where a slope fails completely, the radar echo is scrambled, which shows up as a loss of coherence.

why.title: Where does NISAR fit?
why.body: NISAR started collecting data in 2025, so it did not see the 2014 slide. The story would use older radar archives for the past, and NISAR's 12-day repeat for watching similar slopes now. Which archive covers Oso before 2014 is still to be checked.

why.title: What can the map not tell us?
why.body: Landslides are small, fast and steep. Radar sees only motion along its slanted line of sight, trees weaken the signal, and a slope can fail faster than any satellite returns. Radar is one tool next to field mapping and lidar.

tour.title: Oso, Washington
tour.text: A small valley in Snohomish County, where State Route 530 follows the North Fork Stillaguamish River.

tour.title: A hill under strain
tour.text: The slope above the river had failed before. After weeks of heavy rain, it was saturated. (The radar data here is a placeholder.)

tour.title: March 22, 2014
tour.text: At about 10:37 a.m. the hillside gave way. Debris crossed the river valley in a matter of moments.

tour.title: Could radar have seen it?
tour.text: Comparing two radar passes shows slow creep on the hillside before it failed. Orange means moving away from the satellite. (Placeholder pattern.)

tour.title: Where the radar goes blind
tour.text: Right where the ground collapsed, the radar echo is scrambled. That loss of signal marks the slide itself.

tour.title: Watching slopes today
tour.text: NISAR returns every 12 days. The same method could track the slow creep of slopes like this one, and flag the ones that change.
